## Digital Marketing Agency in Pune: Enhanced Conversions and Consent Mode for Lead-Generation Google Ads, Explained for Business Owners

Enhanced Conversions for leads and Consent Mode v2 are two settings that decide how much of your real enquiry data Google Ads can see. Enhanced Conversions for leads lets your website tag pass a securely hashed email address from a lead form to Google, so a form submission can be matched back to the ad interaction that produced it. Consent Mode tells Google's tags how to behave depending on what each visitor chose in your cookie banner. If either is missing or misconfigured, your account reports fewer leads than you actually receive, and Smart Bidding learns from a thinner, noisier signal. A good digital marketing agency in Pune should be able to show you, on screen, that both are working, not just say so in a report.

This article is for owners and marketing leads who run, or pay for, Google Ads aimed at enquiries: service businesses, clinics, coaching institutes, B2B suppliers. It covers what each feature is, why accounts lose conversion data, how the pieces fit with Google Analytics 4 (GA4) and Google Tag Manager (GTM), what to ask your agency to verify, how to check the work, the India DPDP angle, a checklist and a 30-day rollout.

Technical statements below come from Google Ads Help, Google Analytics Help, Tag Manager Help and the Google Tag Platform documentation, read in October 2026; Google changes these pages often, so confirm current wording before a developer acts. The legal section is general information, not legal advice. We quote no uplift figures, because nobody can promise a fixed percentage from these settings.

## The problem in one picture: the lead you paid for but cannot see

Imagine a Pune physiotherapy clinic running Google Ads. A person clicks an ad, fills in the enquiry form and the receptionist calls back. The account should show one conversion for that keyword. It can fail to: the visitor declined the cookie banner, a tag fired before the consent choice was known, the form submits in the background so the tag never runs, or the enquiry becomes a paying patient two weeks later and that outcome never returns to Google.

Consent Mode and Enhanced Conversions address the first three. The last is offline conversion import, covered in our article on [lead quality and offline conversions](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-lead-quality-offline-conversions-2026). Enhanced Conversions for leads connects the two: it captures the hashed email at form submission so a later qualified lead can be matched back.

## What Enhanced Conversions for leads is

Google's help documentation describes enhanced conversions for leads as a way to improve conversion measurement by supplementing your existing conversion tags with securely hashed first-party customer data collected on your website, for example from a lead form. The hashing uses SHA256, a one-way method: Google can compare a hashed value against hashed values from signed-in Google accounts, but the original email cannot be read back out of the hash. Google then matches the hashed data with signed-in Google accounts to attribute your campaign conversions to ad events such as clicks or views.

### Two stages, not one

Per Google's setup overview, there are two stages:

1. **On the website.** When someone submits the lead form, your tag captures the user-provided data, mainly the email address, hashes it and sends it to Google with the conversion.
2. **After the lead matures.** When a lead later becomes a qualified lead or a sale in your CRM or spreadsheet, you import that outcome into Google Ads, using bulk upload, the Google Ads API or a supported integration such as Salesforce, together with the matching hashed customer information. Google uses it to attribute the offline result back to the original ad interaction.

So it is not just a tracking tweak: it is the bridge between "someone filled in a form" and "someone became a customer".

### What data can be used

According to Google's documentation, acceptable user-provided data includes:

| Data | Notes from Google's documentation |
|---|---|
| Email address | Preferred |
| Name and address | First name, last name, postal code and country are required if you use address data; street, city and region are optional |
| Phone number | Must be sent together with an email address or a full address |

If your form does not ask for an email, there is much less for Enhanced Conversions for leads to work with. Ask your agency whether a required email field is reasonable for your audience, weighed against form completion.

### Terms and timing

- You must review and accept Google's customer data terms. Google says user-provided data collection does not begin until the terms are accepted. Someone with account admin access must do this.
- Google says results become visible about 30 days after implementation, and a tag diagnostics report becomes available roughly 72 hours after implementation. Do not judge the setup after two days.

### Three ways to implement

Google lists three methods: the Google tag directly, Google Tag Manager, or the Google Ads API. Whichever is used, your developer needs to know the conversion trigger (for example the thank-you page URL or the form-submit event) and needs to coordinate with whoever maintains the website code.

## What Consent Mode is

Google's developer documentation describes Consent Mode as a way for Google tags to adjust their behaviour based on the consent choices visitors make on your site. It does not show a banner. A separate tool, called a consent management platform (CMP), or your own code, shows the banner and records the choice. Consent Mode is the layer that tells Google's tags what that choice was.

### The four consent signals

| Signal | What it controls (per Google's documentation) |
|---|---|
| `ad_storage` | Whether advertising cookies can be created |
| `analytics_storage` | Whether analytics measurement can store data |
| `ad_user_data` | Whether user data may be sent to Google for advertising purposes |
| `ad_personalization` | Whether personalised advertising, such as remarketing, may be used |

The last two are what people mean by "Consent Mode v2". The Tag Platform documentation notes that, from November 2023, traffic from the European Economic Area needs these two additional signals alongside the original two to comply with Google's EU user consent policy. That EEA rule is not an Indian legal requirement. Whether you need consent signals for Indian visitors is a question about your privacy approach and Indian law, which we return to in the DPDP section.

### Default and update

Implementation boils down to two commands, per Google's documentation:

- A **default** command sets the starting state, before any measurement happens, for example "denied" for all four signals until the visitor chooses.
- An **update** command changes the state after the visitor clicks accept or reject on the banner.

Values are either "granted" or "denied". Developers can set different defaults for different regions using ISO region codes, with the more specific region overriding the broader one. A `wait_for_update` setting, in milliseconds, makes tags wait briefly so the banner has time to report the visitor's choice. This matters because if the default and update are out of order, tags can fire before the choice is known.

### Basic versus advanced

Google's Analytics Help describes two ways of implementing Consent Mode:

- **Basic.** Google tags are blocked from loading until the visitor grants consent. When consent is denied, no data is sent. This respects the choice immediately but gives up the modelling benefits.
- **Advanced.** Google tags load before the banner appears, and when consent is denied they send cookieless pings: measurements without storing cookies. Google says this enables the full modelling capabilities, filling gaps in your data.

Google notes that in Google Ads, basic implementations rely on general models that use non-identifying variables such as browser type and time of day. When `ad_storage` is denied, no advertising cookies are written or read, and IP addresses are used to derive the country but are never logged. Ad-click identifiers can also be redacted with an `ads_data_redaction` setting.

Neither mode is automatically right. That is a decision for you and your advisers; a good agency explains both and records which was chosen and why.

## Why accounts lose conversion data

Common reasons a lead-generation account under-reports:

### 1. No consent signals, or signals sent in the wrong order

If a banner exists but nothing tells Google's tags the visitor's choice, the tags either run as if everything were granted or are blocked entirely by a tag manager rule, depending on how the site was built. Either is a problem. Google's Tag Manager documentation advises sites without consent mode to enable it through a Google-certified CMP or a custom build so that delayed tag loading does not cause data loss.

### 2. Tags fire before the default is set

The default command must run before measurement begins. If the consent code sits lower down the page than the tags, early hits go out without the right state.

### 3. A form that tags cannot see

Many Indian business sites use contact form plugins, embedded third-party forms or forms that submit in the background without reloading the page. A tag set to fire on a thank-you URL never fires if the form shows a message in place. Enhanced Conversions for leads depends on the tag capturing the hashed email at that moment, so it needs a reliable trigger.

### 4. Offline outcomes never come back

Even with perfect form tracking, Google sees only form submissions unless you send later outcomes. Without them, the algorithm cannot tell a serious enquiry from a time-waster.

### 5. Duplicate or conflicting tags

A site with both a hard-coded Google tag and a GTM-deployed one, or two conversion actions counting the same form, double counts or confuses diagnostics. Our [GA4 conversion tracking guide](/blog/ga4-conversion-tracking-setup-india) covers why installing the Google tag once matters.

## How the pieces fit: GA4, GTM and Google Ads

Who does what:

- **Your website or CMP** shows the banner and records the choice.
- **Consent Mode** passes that choice to Google tags as the four signals.
- **Google Tag Manager** (or the Google tag placed directly) holds the tags and the rules about when they run. GTM can hold the consent configuration alongside the tags.
- **GA4** measures site behaviour and can mark events such as a form submission as key events. GA4 and Google Ads can both record the lead, and they do not always agree, which our GA4 guide explains.
- **The Google Ads conversion tag**, with Enhanced Conversions for leads switched on, records the form submission with the hashed email.
- **Your CRM or sheet** records what happened to each lead later, and is the source for importing outcomes.

The key practical rule: decide which conversion action Google Ads will optimise on, and make sure it is counted once. A typical, careful setup uses the form submission (with Enhanced Conversions for leads) as the main action, and imports qualified or won outcomes as separate, clearly named actions. Ask the agency to draw this on one page for you.

## What a business owner should ask the agency to verify

Ask for dated screenshots or a screen share, not an email saying "done".

1. **Which conversion action does the account optimise on, and how is it counted?** One lead should equal one conversion, with an agreed counting setting.
2. **Is Enhanced Conversions for leads switched on, and have the customer data terms been accepted?** Who accepted them and when?
3. **What does the Google Ads diagnostics report say?** Status for each conversion action, plus any warnings.
4. **Is the default set before any Google tag fires?** Shown in Tag Assistant, not assumed.
5. **Does the banner choice actually change the tags?** Test with accept and with reject, and show the difference.
6. **How does the offline import work, how often, and who does it?** Weekly manual upload from a spreadsheet is a legitimate start for a small business; a CRM integration is better when volume justifies it.
7. **What personal data is being sent, and is it in your privacy notice?** Your notice should say you use contact details for advertising measurement.
8. **Who has admin access to the Google Ads account, GA4 property and GTM container?** You should own them, not the agency. Our [onboarding and access checklist](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-onboarding-access-tracking-checklist-2026) explains how.

If an agency cannot answer questions 3, 4 and 5 with evidence, treat the setup as unverified.

## Diagnostics: how to check in Google Ads and Tag Assistant

### In Google Ads

Google Ads has a diagnostics area for conversions. Google says it shows statuses such as "Recording" and "Needs attention" for each conversion action, and that after you set up Consent Mode you can track compliance status in the conversion diagnostics tab. For Enhanced Conversions for leads, Google says a tag diagnostics report becomes available about 72 hours after implementation, letting you review health checks and metrics.

What to look for:

- A conversion action stuck on "Needs attention", and the reason given.
- A conversion action with zero recorded conversions after your site has had real enquiries. That usually means the trigger is wrong.
- Whether enhanced conversions show as active for the leads action.

### In Tag Assistant

Tag Assistant is Google's debugging tool for tags: in preview mode you interact with your site and see which tags fired. For consent testing, ask your agency to follow this process:

1. Open the site in a fresh browser session so no earlier choice is stored.
2. Before touching the banner, check that the consent default is shown as set, and that Google tags are behaving as the chosen mode expects.
3. Click "reject" or the equivalent, submit a test lead, and note what fired.
4. Repeat in a fresh session with "accept" and note the difference.
5. Check that the consent update appears after the click, and not before.

Google's documentation says Tag Assistant has consent mode debugging tools; we did not find a precise description of its screens in the pages we read, so ask your agency to show you the current view.

## India, consent and the DPDP Act: a general note

This section is general information, not legal advice. If your business handles sensitive customer data, such as health records, take advice from a qualified lawyer.

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 was followed by the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, published in the Gazette on 14 November 2025. According to legal commentaries, including a summary by the law firm JSA, the Rules are phasing in: provisions on the Data Protection Board came into force at once, consent manager provisions follow after about a year (around November 2026), and most obligations on organisations that collect data, such as notice, consent and security safeguards, apply after about 18 months (around May 2027). We cannot confirm every date ourselves, so check the official Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology publications or take legal advice before relying on them.

What this means for advertising measurement, in practical terms:

- **Design for it now.** If the main obligations arrive in 2027, a tracking setup built today should not need a rebuild then. A banner that gives visitors a real choice, and tags that respect it, is a sensible direction regardless of the exact date.
- **Say what you do.** Your privacy notice should explain, in plain language, that you collect contact details through forms and may use them for advertising measurement.
- **Collect only what you need.** Enhanced Conversions for leads needs an email; it does not need an ID number or health details. Never put sensitive details in fields passed to ad platforms.

For more on the website side, see our guide to [what the DPDP Rules mean for a Pune business website](/blog/dpdp-act-website-compliance-pune-2026), and for the remarketing side see [building remarketing audiences with consent in mind](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-remarketing-audiences-consent-2026).

## The checklist

**Measurement foundations:** one Google tag installation; a single named primary lead conversion, counted once; GA4 key events for form, phone and WhatsApp; click identifiers and UTMs reaching the CRM or sheet.

**Enhanced Conversions for leads:** customer data terms accepted; feature active on the leads action; email captured with a tested trigger; diagnostics checked after about 72 hours; offline import agreed and scheduled.

**Consent Mode:** CMP configured and banner wording reviewed; default set before any Google tag fires; all four signals present; basic or advanced chosen and recorded; accept and reject paths tested in Tag Assistant.

**Governance:** privacy notice describes advertising measurement; you own the Google Ads, GA4 and GTM accounts; someone checks diagnostics monthly; a change log is kept.

## A 30-day rollout

A sensible sequence for a small lead-generation account; your agency may adjust it.

### Days 1 to 5: audit and decide

- Gather access to Google Ads, GA4, GTM and the website.
- List every conversion action and tag; pause duplicates after agreeing with your agency.
- Record the current diagnostics state.
- Decide the primary conversion and what a qualified lead means for you.
- Choose basic or advanced Consent Mode and a CMP, and write down why.

### Days 6 to 17: build, test, go live

- Set up the CMP with consent default and update in the right order.
- Configure the form-submission trigger and Enhanced Conversions for leads; accept the customer data terms.
- Run Tag Assistant accept and reject tests on staging if possible, and keep screenshots.
- Submit test leads, confirm they reach your inbox or CRM and register as conversions, then publish.

### Days 18 to 24: confirm and reconcile

- Check the tag diagnostics report, available about 72 hours after implementation.
- Run the weekly three-way comparison of CRM or inbox, Google Ads and GA4.
- Fix anything flagged "Needs attention".

### Days 25 to 30: connect outcomes

- Run the first offline import of qualified and won leads with the matching hashed information, by bulk upload or API.
- Agree monthly reporting: leads, qualified leads, cost per qualified lead and diagnostics status.
- Google says results appear about 30 days after implementation, so judge performance after that.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the difference between Enhanced Conversions for leads and Consent Mode?

Enhanced Conversions for leads sends a securely hashed email or other first-party data from your lead form to Google so conversions can be matched to ads. Consent Mode tells Google's tags what each visitor chose in your cookie banner so the tags behave accordingly. They solve different problems, and a lead-generation account normally needs both set up correctly.

### Do I need Consent Mode v2 if my customers are only in India?

Google's documentation frames the two extra v2 signals around its EU user consent policy for European Economic Area traffic. For India-only audiences it is not a Google requirement, but many businesses adopt it as good practice because it lets the banner choice control advertising tags. Confirm your own obligations under Indian law with a qualified adviser.

### How long before Enhanced Conversions for leads shows results?

Google says a tag diagnostics report becomes available about 72 hours after implementation and that results are visible about 30 days after implementing. Use the diagnostics report early to check the tag is working, and judge performance only after the longer window.

### Does Google see my customers' email addresses?

Google's documentation says the data is hashed with SHA256, a one-way method, before it is sent, and is matched against hashed values from signed-in Google accounts. You still need to describe this use in your privacy notice and accept Google's customer data terms before collection begins.

### What is the first thing I should ask my agency to show me?

Ask for the Google Ads conversion diagnostics screen for your lead conversion action, plus a Tag Assistant test showing what fires when a visitor accepts and when they reject. Those two pieces of evidence reveal most of the common problems quickly.
